chunks.title: Help: Install RadiusPilot on Windows › What you need
chunks.text:
- Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit
- Microsoft Edge WebView2. Up-to-date Windows 10 and 11 already have it
- An internet connection for real scans, website checks and most tools
- To send email: your mailbox address and an app password. See Connect your mailbox (/help/connect-mailbox/)
- Nothing for AI: RadiusPilot AI is included. To use your own account instead: Codex on your PC, a ChatGPT account or an OpenAI API key. See AI Builder drafts (/help/ai-builder/#ai)

chunks.title: Help: Install RadiusPilot on Windows › Install the app
chunks.text:
1. Download the zip: Get it from the download page (/download/). It’s about 9 MB, with RadiusPilot.exe and a short README in English and French.
2. Extract it: Right-click the zip, choose Extract All, then open the folder.
3. Open RadiusPilot.exe: There’s no installer. The app runs from that folder.
4. If Windows says it protected your PC: Choose More info, then Run anyway. Windows asks because RadiusPilot isn’t code-signed yet.
Your data doesn’t live in that folder. The app keeps it in %LOCALAPPDATA%\RadiusPilot: your account, your workspaces, your mailbox and your AI sign-in.

chunks.title: Help: Install RadiusPilot on Windows › The first time you open it
chunks.text:
Create your account. It lives on this computer only and starts on an empty workspace. To look around first, open the live demo (/demo/) on this website: everything in it is invented.
A short setup follows: you, your workspace, what you sell, your plan and, if you like, two-step verification.

chunks.title: Help: Install RadiusPilot on Windows › Updates
chunks.text: RadiusPilot doesn’t update itself yet. The changelog (/changelog/) lists each new version. Download it from the download page (/download/). Your workspaces stay where they are.

chunks.title: Help: Your first scan › Run a scan
chunks.text:
1. Open New scan: Click New scan at the top of the sidebar, or press Ctrl N.
2. Type a place: An address, a street, a neighbourhood or a city. Then pick one of the suggestions.
3. Set the radius: Real scans reach up to 5 km. Quick picks: 0.5, 1, 2, 3 and 5 km. Switch to miles if you prefer.
4. Pick the kinds of businesses: Any of 18: dentists, restaurants, cafés, gyms and studios, hair salons, spas, auto repair, plumbers, HVAC, roofers, law firms, real estate, veterinarians, medical clinics, chiropractors, bakeries, boutiques and hotels.
5. Run it: Add it to a project if you like. Then click Run real scan, or Run preview scan on Starter. Ctrl Enter works too.

chunks.title: Help: Your first scan › What you get
chunks.text:
- The businesses found, nearest first: up to 500 per scan on paid plans, 100 on Starter
- In the Windows app, up to 300 of their homepages checked
- A score for each business, with its reasons
- Every business on ScopeMap (/help/scopemap/)

chunks.title: Help: Your first scan › The preview scan
chunks.text:
On the Starter plan, your first real scan is a preview. It shows how many businesses it found, how many score high, and up to three of them: the ones with the lowest scores. Their phones and websites, and the rest of the list, open on a paid plan.
Starter has no other real scans. Bring in the businesses you already know with Import CSV, on Businesses or Clients, or choose a paid plan to scan more.
A real scan that fails or finds nothing doesn’t use up a scan. Run it again.
[Note] Coverage varies: Some streets are listed in detail, others barely. A business with no website listed may still have one, so check before you pitch. See Where the businesses come from (/help/business-data/).

chunks.text:
The live demo’s markets have ratings, reviews, demand and competitors, so you can see the whole product. Real listings have none of these. For real businesses, those fields stay empty instead of being made up.
That’s why Competitors and the gap zones on ScopeMap only show in the live demo. Competitors is off the menu for now: open it from Ctrl K.

chunks.title: Help: Real data, and the live demo › Why the tools never check demo businesses

The web app is RadiusPilot itself, running in a browser on your computer. There’s nothing to install, and your account and workspaces stay in that browser. Open it from the Web app page (/web/).

chunks.title: Help: Use RadiusPilot in your browser › Get started
chunks.text:
1. Open it on a computer: Choose Open RadiusPilot on the Web app page (/web/). On a phone or a tablet, the page offers to send you the link for your PC instead.
2. Create your account: Type your email on the sign-in screen: a new address goes on to create your account, with your name and a password.
3. Set up your workspace: The first-run setup asks for your workspace’s name, your city and a plan, then you can run your first scan (/help/first-scan/).
[Note] Sign in with your email: The web app has no Google sign-in: its account is the one you create with your email and a password. It’s separate from your account on this website (/help/website-account/), even if you signed in there with Google.

chunks.title: Help: Use RadiusPilot in your browser › What runs in the browser
chunks.text:
- Real scans and their scores, ScopeMap, Businesses and Analytics
- Sequences, offers, proposals and the email builder. Each email opens ready to send in your Gmail, Outlook or mail app: a browser can’t connect your mailbox
- Automations, while the tab is open
- RadiusPilot AI for emails, pitches, reports and proposals, with your plan’s credits (/help/credits/)
- AI Builder decks and reports. Websites and the website editor are coming soon, in beta (/beta/)
- Site speed, Email health, Site history, QR codes and Post maker, and Brand kit from a logo file
- CSV import and export, backups, and two-step verification

chunks.title: Help: Use RadiusPilot in your browser › What needs the Windows app
chunks.text:
A web page can’t read other websites or reach your mailbox, so these run only in the Windows app (/download/), a test version that hasn’t run on a real Windows computer yet:
- The website checks during a scan (HTTPS, mobile layout, booking and the rest), and the website audit’s read of a site
- Site technology and Published contacts (/help/published-contacts/)
- Brand kit from a website’s own styles
- Sending from your own mailbox. See Connect your mailbox (/help/connect-mailbox/)
- Your own AI account instead of RadiusPilot AI: Codex, ChatGPT or an OpenAI API key
- Workspaces saved as files on your computer
Scores in the browser come from each business’s public listing. The Windows app adds what it finds on their websites.

chunks.title: Help: Use RadiusPilot in your browser › Where your data lives
chunks.text:
Your account (your name, your email and a salted hash of your password, plus your authenticator key if you turn on two-step verification) and your workspaces are saved in this browser’s storage for radiuspilot.com, on this device. None of it goes to a RadiusPilot server. Settings › Data shows where it is and how much room it takes.
- Another browser, another browser profile or another computer starts empty: nothing syncs yet
- Clearing your browser’s data for radiuspilot.com deletes your account and your workspaces
- A forgotten password can’t be reset by email: the account lives only in this browser
- In a private window, everything may be lost when the window closes
[Warning] Keep a backup: Download a backup from Settings › Data now and then, and keep the file somewhere safe: it holds your contacts.

chunks.title: Help: Use RadiusPilot in your browser › Move to the Windows app
chunks.text:
1. Download a backup: In the web app, open Settings › Data and choose Download backup, protected with a password you choose. You get one file per workspace: repeat it in each one.
2. Open the Windows app: Create your account there, then open the workspace to fill. See Install RadiusPilot on Windows (/help/install/).
3. Restore it: In Settings › Data, under Restore from a backup, choose the file, type its password, then Replace and restore. It replaces that workspace, and you can undo.
Backups never include passwords, your mailbox or AI keys. Use the same version of RadiusPilot on both sides: a backup from a newer version asks you to update the app first.

chunks.title: Help: Where the businesses come from › What a scan finds
chunks.text:
Each business comes with what its listing has:
- Its name, its kind of business and its position
- Often an address, a phone number, a website and opening hours
- Sometimes an email address and links to social pages
The scan keeps the nearest businesses, up to your plan’s limit. In the Windows app, it then checks up to 300 of their homepages. See What the website checks look at (/help/website-checks/).

chunks.title: Help: Where the businesses come from › Why coverage varies
chunks.text: New scans list businesses from Google Maps, through RadiusPilot’s server. Most businesses are there, but a listing can be out of date: a missing website or phone may only be missing from the listing, so check before you pitch.

chunks.title: Help: Where the businesses come from › What stays empty
chunks.text:
A business’s rating and review count come from Google, labelled as Google’s, only when Google has them: a business with no reviews shows none, never 0 stars. Search rankings and SEO stay empty. RadiusPilot never makes any of them up. The score uses only the facts it has: see How the opportunity score works (/help/opportunity-score/).
[Note] Google data, the official way: Everything from Google comes through Google’s official Places API and is labelled as Google’s. RadiusPilot never copies it from Google’s pages.

chunks.title: Help: Where the businesses come from › Credit
chunks.text: Google’s name sits next to its ratings and reviews, in the map’s corner and in exports, as its terms ask. Businesses from older scans keep the credit their open data’s licence asks for, in the map’s corner, Settings › About and exported reports. If you share the data elsewhere, keep those credits: see the terms (/terms/#third-parties).

chunks.title: Help: How the opportunity score works
chunks.text:
What the score weighs for real businesses, and what High, Medium and Low mean.
Every business gets a score from 0 to 100. The higher it is, the more the business is missing that an agency can fix. Its reasons sit next to it, so you can explain the number to the owner.
Help center, Scores and checks. Updated November 3, 2026.
Search terms: opportunity score scoring weights presets high medium low tiers best opportunities scoring rules imported custom confidence chain website audit

chunks.title: Help: How the opportunity score works › What counts for real businesses
chunks.text:
For real businesses the score uses facts only: the public listing, the homepage check in the Windows app and any website audit. A missing or broken website weighs most, and more for the kinds of businesses people usually choose online.
Weighs | Facts:
- Most: No website (a little less when a social page stands in for one), or a website that doesn’t load
- A lot: No mobile layout, a slow site, no HTTPS or a bad certificate
- Some: A site nobody updates, few ways to call or book, no page title or description, an outdated platform, weak email setup and other audit findings
- A little: No visitor analytics, no social profiles, accessibility problems, and missing opening hours, phone or address
Part of a chain takes points off, since head office may decide on its website. Where a website audit and the homepage check overlap, the audit wins.
Facts not checked yet count as typical, never as good or bad, and the score says how sure it is: high, medium or low confidence. Gaps add up, then level off, so no business sits at a flat 100. Equal scores rank by confidence, then by distance.

chunks.title: Help: How the opportunity score works › High, Medium and Low
chunks.text: High is 60 and up, Medium 40 to 59, Low under 40. Move the thresholds in Businesses › Best opportunities, under Scoring rules: High from 40 to 90, Medium from 15 to 70.

chunks.title: Help: How the opportunity score works › Presets and custom weights
chunks.text:
Real businesses always use the fixed model above: presets and custom weights don’t change it. For businesses from Google, a low rating or few reviews adds to the score, from Google’s own figures, and a business without them is never scored as if it had bad ones. The High and Medium thresholds apply to every business.
The weights are for the live demo (/demo/)’s markets, which weigh nine factors, including ratings, reviews and demand. Four presets set them: Balanced, Local SEO, Reputation and Web design. Change any weight, from 0 to 3, and the preset becomes Custom.
Businesses imported from your own file aren’t scored. Your file has no website checks, ratings or reviews, so they show a dash instead of a number.
[Note] Never made up: Ratings, reviews and search rankings stay empty for real businesses. When Google data arrives through Google’s official Places API, it will be labelled as Google’s.

chunks.title: Help: What the website checks look at
chunks.text:
During a scan, the Windows app opens each homepage once and notes a few facts. A website audit checks much more.
In the Windows app, a scan checks up to 300 homepages, four at a time. Each check is one ordinary page request, like a visitor’s, with an 8-second limit.
Help center, Scores and checks. Updated October 27, 2026.

chunks.title: Help: What the website checks look at › What it notes
chunks.text:
- Whether the site uses HTTPS with a valid certificate
- Whether the page is set up for phones (a mobile viewport)
- Booking links: 46 booking services, and “book online” words in six languages
- The copyright year in the footer
- The page title and description
- The website builder the page names, and its links to social pages
- The page size, and how long it took to load from your computer

chunks.title: Help: What the website checks look at › What it doesn’t do
chunks.text:
- Run Google’s speed test. Use Site speed (/tools/#speed) or a website audit for that
- Read other pages, fill in forms or sign in anywhere
- Open addresses on private networks

chunks.title: Help: What the website checks look at › A full website audit
chunks.text:
Run audit in a profile, or Website audit in Tools, runs every check together: Google’s speed test on a phone and a computer, Email health, Site technology, Site history and, in the Windows app, a read of the site itself. It grades the site from A to F, scores each section, and lists fixes and pitch lines built only from what was found.
In Tools, audit any website address, or a whole scan, a market or a selection with Audit several.
A check that doesn’t answer adds nothing to the grade. Site technology and the read of the site need the Windows app. Demo businesses get an audit built from their demo data, with nothing checked, and it says so.

chunks.title: Help: What the website checks look at › When checks stop
chunks.text:
After six network failures in a row, the scan stops checking websites and keeps the listings. One bad connection won’t ruin a scan.
[Note] Load time isn’t a speed score: It’s how long your computer took to fetch the page. Google’s scores come from Site speed (/tools/#speed).

chunks.title: Help: Connect your mailbox
chunks.text:
Send and receive from your own address in the Windows app. Your password stays encrypted on your computer.
RadiusPilot sends from your own mailbox. Replies come back to you, and your provider’s rules apply. Real mail works in the Windows app once you connect. Until then, and in the web app, RadiusPilot doesn’t send by itself: Open in Gmail (or Outlook, or your mail app) opens the email ready to send, personalised and with its footer, or save it as a draft, or Copy it. In the live demo, sends to its invented addresses are simulated.

chunks.title: Help: Connect your mailbox › Before you start
chunks.text: Most providers want an app password for apps like RadiusPilot, not your usual password. Gmail, iCloud, Yahoo and Fastmail do. Create one in your account’s security settings. The hint under App password says what your provider needs.

chunks.title: Help: Connect your mailbox › Connect
chunks.text:
1. Open Settings, then Email: Or press Ctrl , and pick Email.
2. Choose your provider: Gmail, Outlook.com, Microsoft 365, iCloud Mail, Yahoo Mail, Zoho Mail or Fastmail. For any other, choose IMAP / SMTP.
3. Enter your details: Your email address, your name as people see it, and the app password.
4. Add the servers, for IMAP / SMTP: Open Server settings. Add the incoming and outgoing servers, their ports and the security: SSL/TLS or STARTTLS.
5. Click Connect: RadiusPilot signs in to check it works. Nothing is sent.

chunks.title: Help: Connect your mailbox › Your password
chunks.text: Windows encrypts it for your Windows account, and it stays on this computer, in RadiusPilot’s folder. It’s never written to a log. Disconnect removes the password, the settings and the cached mail. Your email stays with your provider.

chunks.title: Help: Connect your mailbox › How much to send
chunks.text:
The daily limit counts people, not emails: one email to three people uses three. It starts at 50 a day. Set it from 10 to 200 in Settings › Email. New mailboxes do best starting around 30 to 50 people a day, then growing slowly.
One email goes to 50 people at most, To, Cc and Bcc together. The Windows app also refuses more than 200 people a day, whatever the setting.

chunks.title: Help: Connect your mailbox › Images in emails you receive
chunks.text: Images from other senders stay hidden until you click Show images, because loading them tells the sender you opened the email. Choose Always for a sender to show theirs every time. Links open in your browser, and only web, email and phone links open.

chunks.title: Help: Email rules: CASL and CAN-SPAM
chunks.text:
What RadiusPilot adds to help you follow anti-spam law, and what stays your job.
[Warning] Not legal advice: This is general information. Ask a lawyer about your own outreach.
Help center, Outreach. Updated October 27, 2026.
Search terms: casl can-spam anti-spam law consent implied unsubscribe opt-out list-unsubscribe footer mailing address postal address canada united states

chunks.title: Help: Email rules: CASL and CAN-SPAM › What RadiusPilot adds to every email
chunks.text:
- Your business name and postal address, then this line: Don’t want emails like this? Reply “unsubscribe” and we won’t email you again.
- A List-Unsubscribe header on outreach, when the email goes out right away
- A block on every address in your opt-out list, also when you copy an email to send elsewhere
- A stop at your daily limit, counted in people
Every email gets the line, emails to your clients too. It can’t be switched off, and it’s added even when a template has its own unsubscribe link. The Windows app refuses to send an email without it.

chunks.title: Help: Email rules: CASL and CAN-SPAM › What stays your job
chunks.text:
- Add your business’s postal address in Settings › Email. It starts empty, and outreach from your mailbox waits until it’s there
- Add everyone who asks to stop to the opt-out list
- Write to businesses about things that relate to their work
- Keep a record of where you found each address. Published contacts (/help/published-contacts/) saves the page and the date with the address you use

chunks.title: Help: Email rules: CASL and CAN-SPAM › Canada: CASL
chunks.text: Canada’s anti-spam law covers commercial email received in Canada, wherever the sender is. You need consent. Implied consent can cover an address a business publishes conspicuously, without saying it doesn’t want unsolicited email, when your message relates to its business or the person’s role. Guessed or harvested addresses don’t have it.

chunks.title: Help: Email rules: CASL and CAN-SPAM › United States: CAN-SPAM
chunks.text: CAN-SPAM lets you email businesses without prior consent. The email must not mislead. It must say it’s an ad when it is one, include a valid postal address, and offer an opt-out that you honour within 10 business days.

chunks.title: Help: Email rules: CASL and CAN-SPAM › Other places
chunks.text: Rules differ elsewhere, and Europe’s are much stricter. Check before you write to businesses outside Canada and the United States.

chunks.title: Help: Sequences, follow-ups and automations

Sequences plan your follow-ups and wait for you. Automations run the steps you choose.
A sequence is a plan for one lead: emails, calls and tasks, each on a day after the start, up to day 90. Sequences live in a tab of Automations.

- Cold intro: an intro email, a call three days later, a follow-up on day 7 and a polite break-up on day 14
- Audit follow-up: an email, a call on day 2, a task on day 5 and an email on day 9

chunks.title: Help: Sequences, follow-ups and automations › How steps run
chunks.text:
A due step waits for you in Today. You send the email or make the call. Nothing goes out on its own.
A reply ends the sequence for that lead, so nobody gets a follow-up after answering. That’s the Stop when they reply switch, on by default.

chunks.title: Help: Sequences, follow-ups and automations › Calls
chunks.text: Call mode lines up the next people to call, with tap-to-call links. Keys 1 to 7 log how each call went. RadiusPilot doesn’t place or record calls.

chunks.title: Help: Sequences, follow-ups and automations › Automations
chunks.text:
An automation starts from a trigger, such as a finished scan, a reply or a schedule. Then it runs the steps you pick: find leads, run a website audit, write an email, wait for your approval, add a task. Start from a template, or describe it in a sentence.
Automations run while RadiusPilot is open. Approvals wait for you in Today.
A send step saves drafts unless you switch it to Send. Every email it sends still gets your unsubscribe line, and respects the opt-out list and the daily limit.

Websites, pitch decks, market reports and lead lists, drafted from what a scan found, then edited in the website editor.
AI Builder drafts a first version for a business from your scans: a website, a pitch deck, a market report or a lead list. Your market reports live in its Reports tab.
[Note] The website builder is in beta: Website drafts and the website editor are coming soon to everyone. Request beta access (/beta/) to try them first: the app’s website builder asks for your beta code.

chunks.title: Help: AI Builder drafts › How drafts are written
chunks.text:
RadiusPilot AI is included, in the web app and the Windows app, with nothing to connect: it writes the words on the pitch-deck slides and the sentences around a report’s figures, and for beta testers it designs the website, its pages, sections and copy. The figures stay RadiusPilot’s own. Each task uses a few of your plan’s credits (/help/credits/).
What you ask RadiusPilot AI to write goes to our server, then to our AI provider in the United States. We don’t keep it. The privacy policy (/privacy/#app) names the provider and has the details.
When no AI can write, as in the live demo, drafts start from templates, filled in with the business’s facts: its name, its kind of business, its area and what the scan found.

chunks.title: Help: Where your data lives, and how to remove it › On your computer
chunks.text:
The app stores your accounts, workspaces, businesses, emails and settings on your computer. Each workspace is one file in %LOCALAPPDATA%\RadiusPilot\workspaces, with the version before each save kept next to it. Windows encrypts these files for your Windows account: another Windows user on the PC, or someone who copies the disk, gets unreadable files. The app sends none of it to us.
Because of that encryption, a workspace file copied to another computer or another Windows account can’t be opened there. To move a workspace, use a backup file.
The web app keeps the same things in your browser’s storage for radiuspilot.com instead. See Use RadiusPilot in your browser (/help/web-app/#data).

Only what a feature needs, when you use it:
Service | What it receives, and when:

- Each business’s website: One ordinary page request during a scan, and when you run a tool or a website audit on it. Published contacts reads up to five more pages of the same site. The website audit also reads the homepage’s stylesheets, robots.txt, the sitemap, the plain-HTTP address and up to two contact or about pages. Site technology and the Brand kit tool read the homepage’s stylesheets too. In the web app, these reads go through our server, which reads the page and sends it back; it keeps only a count per connection, keyed by a hash of its IP address

Our server answers it the way the app’s features do: the listing services for a business search, the website for a site check, RadiusPilot AI for drafts and reports. It keeps a hash of each key, when it was last used, and a log of each request for 30 days, never what you asked RadiusPilot AI to write

chunks.title: Guide: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score?
chunks.text:
A Performance score of 90 to 100 is good. What the bands mean, why the score is a lab test, why it moves between runs, and what Google actually measures.
Published November 3, 2026. Topic: Audits.
In PageSpeed Insights, a Performance score of 90 to 100 is good, 50 to 89 needs improvement and 0 to 49 is poor. That score comes from a simulated lab test, though: how real visitors experience the page is the Core Web Vitals assessment at the top of the report.
In short:
- 90 to 100 is good, 50 to 89 needs improvement, 0 to 49 is poor.
- The score is lab data from Lighthouse. The top of the report is real Chrome users over 28 days.
- Real visitors pass when LCP is 2.5 s or less, INP 200 ms or less and CLS 0.1 or less, at the 75th percentile.
- The score moves between runs: test a few times and look at the range.
- Google says a good score doesn’t guarantee top rankings.

chunks.title: Guide: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score? › The three score bands

Score | Band:
- 90 to 100: Good (green)
- 50 to 89: Needs improvement (orange)
- 0 to 49: Poor (red)
Phones and computers get separate results, on separate tabs. Always say which one you’re quoting.

chunks.title: Guide: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score? › What the score is made of
chunks.text:
PageSpeed Insights runs Lighthouse on the address in a simulated environment, then weighs five lab measures. These are the weights Chrome’s Lighthouse documentation lists first:
Lab measure | Weight:
- Total Blocking Time: 30%
- Largest Contentful Paint: 25%
- Cumulative Layout Shift: 25%
- First Contentful Paint: 10%
- Speed Index: 10%
Only these measures count. The opportunities and diagnostics further down suggest fixes, but they don’t change the score.

chunks.title: Guide: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score? › Real visitors come first
chunks.text:
When Google has enough visits, the top of the report shows field data: real Chrome users over the previous 28 days. The page passes the Core Web Vitals assessment when the 75th percentile of all three measures is good. If INP has too little data, LCP and CLS decide.
- Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): the main image or text block appears within 2.5 seconds.
- Interaction to Next Paint (INP): the page reacts to a tap or click in 200 milliseconds or less.
- Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): the layout moves by 0.1 or less while it loads.
A new page, or one with few visits, may not have enough data. PageSpeed Insights then shows data for the whole site, or no real-user data at all, and the lab score is all you have. The two can disagree: the lab simulates one device and connection, while field data comes from real people on theirs.

chunks.title: Guide: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score? › Why the score changes between runs
chunks.text:
Run the same page twice and the number can move. Chrome’s documentation says much of that variability doesn’t come from Lighthouse itself but from changing conditions, such as:
- A/B tests or ads that change between loads
- Changes in how internet traffic is routed
- Testing on different devices
- Browser extensions that add scripts or change requests
- Antivirus software
It suggests treating performance as a range of scores rather than one number. Run the test a few times, note the lowest and highest, and keep the date.

chunks.title: Guide: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score? › Does a good score help rankings?
chunks.text:
Google recommends good Core Web Vitals “for success with Search” and says they align with what its core ranking systems seek to reward. It also says there is no single page experience signal, that good results in its reports or third-party tools don’t guarantee top rankings, and that Search “always seeks to show the most relevant content, even if the page experience is sub-par.”
So a faster page is better for visitors and fits what Google says it seeks to reward, but a score of 100 is not a ranking.

chunks.title: Guide: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score? › What to watch out for when you quote a score
chunks.text:
- Name the tab and the source. “Mobile, lab test” or “real visitors, last 28 days”.
- Compare like with like. The same page, the same tab, tested the same day.
- Lead with what people notice. “On a phone, your main photo takes longer than Google’s 2.5-second target to appear” means more to an owner than a bare score, as long as the report shows it.
- Promise no score and no ranking. Offer to measure again after the work, the same way.
Speed is one of ten checks in the website audit checklist (/guides/website-audit-checklist/), which also covers HTTPS, the phone layout and booking. Finding local businesses that need a new website (/guides/find-local-businesses-that-need-a-website/) shows where the audit fits in prospecting.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
Ten checks to run on a small business’s website before you pitch: what to look at, how to verify it by hand, and how to turn one finding into a fair email.
Published November 2, 2026. Topic: Audits.
A good pitch to a small business starts with something true about its website that the owner can check in a minute. A vague “your site could be better” gets deleted. “Your booking page doesn’t open on a phone” gets a reply.
This checklist gives you ten checks, in the order that keeps an audit short: what to look at, how to verify it yourself, and what to say about it. It works by hand, with a phone, a browser and Google’s own tools.
In short:
- Run the same ten checks on every site, in the same order, and note the date and the tool.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
- Start with the basics: the site loads, uses HTTPS and works on a phone.
- Quote Google’s speed thresholds, and say whether a number is real-user or lab data.
- Rank what you found, and pitch the one gap that matters most to that business.
- Never promise rankings or invent lost-sales figures: Google warns owners about both.
Search terms: website audit checklist, small business website audit, website review, pitch web design, https, ssl certificate, mobile friendly, viewport, core web vitals, pagespeed insights, field data, lab data, title tag, meta description, alt text, colour contrast, wcag, click to call, online booking, business listing, opening hours, spf, dmarc, agency, freelancer

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › Before you start: one sheet, one order
chunks.text:
Open a spreadsheet with one row per business and one column per check below. For each finding, note the date, the device or tool you used, and a screenshot if you can. Websites change: a record of what you saw, and when, keeps your email accurate and lets you check again before you send.
Audit businesses of the same kind together, such as five dental clinics in one neighbourhood. Patterns show up fast, and you learn what “good” looks like for that trade. If you haven’t built your list yet, start with how to find local businesses that need a new website (/guides/find-local-businesses-that-need-a-website/).

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › The ten checks (part 1 of 6)
chunks.text:
1. Does the site load on its own address?
Type the address yourself, with and without www, and once starting with http://. Each should land on the same working homepage. An expired domain, a parked page, a hosting error or a site that only works under one spelling is the biggest gap there is, and the easiest to explain.
2. HTTPS and its certificate
The address should start with https://, and the http:// version should redirect there. Click the icon left of the address to see whether the connection is secure and the certificate valid. Browsers warn visitors about plain http pages: the find-local guide (/guides/find-local-businesses-that-need-a-website/#check) explains what Chrome shows.
Google’s page experience self-assessment asks, “Are your pages served in a secure fashion?” Yet Google also says it “always seeks to show the most relevant content, even if the page experience is sub-par.” Sell HTTPS as trust, not as a ranking boost. The fix is rarely expensive: Let’s Encrypt, run by the nonprofit Internet Security Research Group, issues certificates at no cost, and many hosts set them up for you.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › The ten checks (part 2 of 6)
chunks.text:
3. On a phone
Open the site on your own phone, not in a narrow desktop window. Can you read the text without zooming? Do buttons work with a thumb? Does anything run off the side of the screen?
Then view the page source on a computer and search for viewport. Without a viewport meta tag such as <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width">, phones may draw the page as if on a wider screen and shrink it to fit, as MDN explains. That’s the tiny-text, pinch-to-zoom look owners recognise.
It matters for search too. Google says it “uses the mobile version of a site’s content” for indexing and ranking, and that the mobile site should have the same content as the desktop one. A phone version that hides the menu, the hours or the services hides them from Google as well.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › The ten checks (part 3 of 6)
chunks.text:
4. Speed, with Google’s own numbers
Paste the address into PageSpeed Insights and read the phone results first. Google’s web.dev sets three Core Web Vitals targets, judged at the 75th percentile of page loads, on phones and computers separately:
What it measures | Good:
- LCP: how long the main image or text block takes to appear: 2.5 s or less
- INP: how quickly the page reacts to a tap or click: 200 ms or less
- CLS: how much the layout jumps while it loads: 0.1 or less
Know which numbers you’re quoting. The top of the report is field data: real Chrome users over the previous 28 days. The scores below are lab data, from a simulated Lighthouse test. A small site may not have enough visitors: PageSpeed Insights then falls back to data for the whole site, or shows no real-user data at all. In that case, quote the lab result and call it a lab test.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › The ten checks (part 4 of 6)
chunks.text:
5. Calling, finding and booking
Check, from the homepage and on a phone, the ways a customer gets in touch or comes in:
- Phone: is the number visible, and is it a tel: link? On a phone, a tel: link lets the visitor call in one tap.
- Address and hours: are they on the site, and current?
- Booking or ordering: for clinics, salons, restaurants and gyms, is there a way to book or order online? How many taps does it take?
- Contact form: does the page exist and load? Don’t send a test message: it lands in a real person’s inbox.
6. Is anyone looking after it?
Look for signs the site has been left alone: a copyright year from years ago in the footer, news or events long past, a menu or price list that contradicts the listing, holiday hours from a previous year, links that lead nowhere. A neglected site can mean nobody owns it any more: a good opening for a care plan, not only a redesign.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › The ten checks (part 5 of 6)
chunks.text:
7. How it shows in search results
Search for the business’s name and look at its result, then view the homepage source for <title> and <meta name="description">.
Google asks for “descriptive and concise” titles, distinct on each page, without the same words repeated. It says it uses the meta description only “sometimes”, when it describes the page better than the page’s own text, and that identical descriptions on every page “aren’t helpful”. A homepage titled “Home”, or every page with the same title, is a clear, fixable finding.
8. Accessibility basics
Two checks anyone can run. First, images: the W3C says images “must have text alternatives that describe the information or function represented by them”, while purely decorative images get an empty alt="". A logo or a “Book now” button made of an image with no alt text is a real problem for screen reader users.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › The ten checks (part 6 of 6)
chunks.text:
Second, contrast: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 (level AA) asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Check light grey text on a white background first. Point it out as readability for every customer, without claiming the business breaks a law.
9. Email setup
A business’s email records are public. Look up its SPF and DMARC records on the email check page (/email-check/), which sends the business nothing. A missing DMARC record means nothing tells mail servers to refuse email that fakes the business’s address. SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained (/guides/spf-dkim-dmarc-explained/) covers what each finding means.
10. Listings match the site
Compare the website with the business’s public map listings and directory pages: name, phone, address, hours and website link. A listing with old hours, a disconnected number or no website link sends customers the wrong way. If the listing shows no website, search the name and city before you conclude there is none.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › Rank what you found
chunks.text:
You may find several gaps. Pitch one, the one that costs the business most. A simple order:
Priority | Gaps:
- First: No website, or one that doesn’t load
- High: No phone layout, slow on a phone, no HTTPS or a bad certificate
- Medium: Hard to call or book, a neglected site, missing or repeated page titles, weak email setup
- Lower: Missing alt text, low contrast, listing details out of date
Weigh the business’s kind too. No online booking is a bigger gap for a salon, where customers book appointments, than for an emergency plumber, who gets calls. A slow site matters more when most customers arrive on phones.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › Turn one finding into a pitch
chunks.text:
Owners have been warned about cold pitches. Google’s own page on hiring an SEO tells them to “be wary of SEO firms and web consultants or agencies that email you out of the blue”, and says “no one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google”. Write the email that passes that test.
1. Say who you are: Your name, your business and that you work nearby.
2. Name one finding and how to see it: “Open your site on your phone and tap Book: the page doesn’t load.” The owner can check it in a minute.
3. Explain it plainly: What a customer sees or can’t do. No invented figures about lost sales, no promises about rankings.
4. Offer the fix and a small next step: What you would change, and a ten-minute call or a one-page summary of what you checked.
In Canada, an email like this also has to follow CASL: an address the business published, a message relevant to its business, your identification and an unsubscribe link. Cold email in Canada (/guides/casl-cold-email-canada/) covers the rules.

chunks.title: Guide: Website audit checklist for pitching a small business › What an audit by hand can’t tell you
chunks.text:
- How many visitors the site gets, or where they come from. Only the owner’s analytics know.
- Why something is the way it is. A slow site may be a cheap host or a heavy theme, and the owner may already know.
- Whether the lab test matches real visitors, when there’s no field data.
- Whether a business has no website, from its listing alone.
Say what you checked, and stop there. An accurate, modest audit earns more trust than a long list of alarms.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website
chunks.text:
A step-by-step method for agencies and freelancers: list one neighbourhood’s businesses, check each website, score the gaps and pitch one real fact.
Published November 1, 2026. Topic: Finding clients.
The businesses that need a new website aren’t hidden. They’re on the streets around you: the clinic with no way to book, the plumber whose site shows “Not secure”. The work is finding them in order, and pitching them with a fact instead of “I build websites”.
Here is a method you can start this week, by hand or with RadiusPilot, in any city.
In short:
- Work one neighbourhood and two or three kinds of business.
- List every business, with where and when you found it.
- Check five things: a website, HTTPS, speed on a phone, online booking and listing details.
- Score the gaps and start at the top.
- Pitch one fact per email, follow up, keep notes and stay within CASL.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Pick one neighbourhood and a few kinds of business
chunks.text:
Start small on purpose. One neighbourhood you can walk and two or three kinds of business give you a list you can finish, and let you compare a dentist’s site with other dentists’ sites.
Choose businesses whose customers look them up before they call or visit: clinics, salons, restaurants, gyms and trades like plumbers or roofers. Pick kinds you know or can show work for: a site you built for one clinic helps you pitch the next.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › List every business in the area
chunks.text:
Use more than one source: each misses businesses the others have.
1. Walk the street: Note each storefront’s name and kind of business, and any phone number, hours or web address on the door. Walking catches new businesses and the ones directories missed.
2. Check local directories: Your chamber of commerce, the business improvement area (a BIA, or an SDC in Québec) and professional associations may publish member directories.
3. Search public map listings: Search the map apps your customers use, for each kind of business in the area, and note what each listing shows.
4. Keep one sheet: One row per business: name, kind, address, phone, website, and where and when you found each detail. That record shows later where an email address came from.
[Note] Missing from the listing isn’t missing: Search the business’s name and city before you write “no website”. Pitching a site to a business that has one is a poor start.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Check each website the same way (part 1 of 3)
chunks.text:
Run the same five checks on every business, in the same order, so you can compare the results.
Does it have a website at all?
No website is the biggest gap, and the easiest to explain. A Facebook or Instagram page standing in for one is a smaller gap. A domain that doesn’t load, or has expired, counts as none.
Does it use HTTPS?
The address should start with https://. Chrome has marked every plain http page “Not secure” since Chrome 68, in July 2018. Since Chrome 154, released in September 2026, it also prompts people by default when they connect to a site over an insecure http connection.
Google’s page experience checklist asks whether pages are served securely, but Google also says it seeks to show the most relevant content even when page experience is sub-par. Sell HTTPS as trust, not as rankings.
Does it load quickly on a phone?

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Check each website the same way (part 2 of 3)
chunks.text:
Google sums up how a page feels to visitors in three Core Web Vitals. In plain words:
- Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): how long the biggest image or block of text on screen takes to appear. Good is within 2.5 seconds.
- Interaction to Next Paint (INP): how quickly the page reacts to a tap, a click or a key press. Good is 200 milliseconds or less.
- Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): how much the layout jumps around unexpectedly, like a button that moves as you tap it. Good is 0.1 or less.
Google judges each at the 75th percentile of page loads, on phones and computers separately: a page passes when at least three loads in four meet each target.
Paste the address into PageSpeed Insights. It shows two things:
- A lab test: Lighthouse loads the page on a simulated mid-tier phone over a mobile network. Its performance score is good at 90 or above, needs improvement from 50 to 89, and is poor below 50.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Check each website the same way (part 3 of 3)
chunks.text:
- Real visits: Chrome users’ Core Web Vitals over the previous 28 days. With too few visits on record, you get the whole site’s figures, or none.
The two can disagree. Quote real visits when there are some; otherwise quote the lab test and say it’s a lab test. Then try the site on your own phone: can you read it without zooming and find the phone number?
Can a customer book or order online?
Count the taps from the homepage to booking an appointment, ordering or asking for a quote. Phone only is a real gap for a salon or a clinic, less so for a roofer who prefers to talk first.
Are the listing details complete?
Look the business up as a customer would, in a map app or a search engine. Are the hours, phone number and website there, and do they match the site?
Google’s help for business owners says complete and accurate information makes a business more likely to show up in local results. It’s a small fix, and a good first job.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Score and sort the list
chunks.text:
Give each gap points, add them up and sort from highest to lowest. One simple scale:
Gap | Points:
- No website, or one that doesn’t load: 5
- No HTTPS, or a certificate that isn’t valid: 2
- LCP over 2.5 seconds, or a lab score under 50: 2
- No online booking where customers expect it: 1
- Each missing listing detail: hours, phone or website: 1
No website takes the 5 plus its listing gaps; the other rows apply only to businesses with a site. Then adjust by hand:
- Move chains and franchises down: head office may decide on the website.
- Break ties by distance: the closer, the easier to meet.
- Skip businesses that look closed, and anyone who asked not to be contacted.
Keep the top ten or twenty for this week.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Write a short pitch that names what you found
chunks.text:
Lead with one concrete fact the owner can check on their own phone in a minute. One fact per email: a list reads like an audit they didn’t ask for. Facts like these:
- Chrome shows “Not secure” next to your address.
- On a phone, your homepage misses Google’s 2.5-second target for its main content, in Google’s own test.
- The phone number is the only way to book.
- Your listing has no opening hours.
Build the email around it:
1. Who you are, and where: Your name, your business, and that you work nearby.
2. The fact, and how to check it: What you found, and how they can see it: “Open your site in Chrome and look at the address bar.”
3. Why it matters: What a customer sees or can’t do, with no invented figures about lost sales.
4. One small next step: A ten-minute call, a one-page summary of what you checked, or a draft homepage.
Use a subject that names the fact, like “Your website shows ‘Not secure’ in Chrome”. Send it from your own mailbox to the address the business publishes, never to a guessed one like firstname.lastname@: the consent below doesn’t cover it.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Follow up, and keep notes
chunks.text:
Plan the follow-ups before the first email, and stop the moment they answer, yes or no. A simple rhythm:
- First, the email with your one fact.
- Three days later, a short call, or a visit if you’re nearby.
- On day 7, a follow-up with a second fact, or the summary you offered.
- On day 14, a polite last note.
Keep notes on every business: what you sent and when, the fact you used, their answer, the next step, and where you found their email address. Put anyone who asks you to stop on an opt-out list, for good.
Your notes also show what works. Count replies per email sent, by kind of business and by the fact you led with, then drop the facts that don’t get answers.

chunks.title: Guide: How to find local businesses that need a new website › Mind the rules
chunks.text:
[Warning] Not legal advice: This is general information about Canada’s anti-spam law. Ask a lawyer about your own outreach.
In Canada, commercial email falls under the anti-spam law, CASL, and you need consent. For a first email to a business, that usually means implied consent from an address it published.
The Government of Canada’s guidance says that works when the address was conspicuously published, without a statement refusing unsolicited commercial messages, and when your message is relevant to the person’s business, role, functions or duties. Every email must also include:
- Your business name, and the name of anyone you’re sending for
- A current mailing address, plus a phone number, an email address or a website, valid for at least 60 days after you send
- An unsubscribe that works, with every request handled within 10 business days, at no cost
If asked, you should be ready to prove consent: that’s what the source and date on your sheet are for. The email rules guide (/help/email-rules/) covers what RadiusPilot adds to every email, and the rules in the United States.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
What Canada’s anti-spam law asks before an agency emails a local business: consent, published addresses, sender details, unsubscribes, records and penalties.
Published November 1, 2026. Topic: Outreach.
You spot a local business with no booking page or an outdated website. You find its email address and write. In Canada, that first email falls under Canada’s anti-spam legislation, known as CASL.
In short:
- A pitch to a business is a commercial electronic message: it needs consent, sender details and an unsubscribe mechanism.
- Implied consent can cover an address a business conspicuously published without refusing unsolicited messages, if your email is relevant to its business or the person’s role.
- Honour every unsubscribe without delay, and within 10 business days at most.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
- The sender has to prove consent, so keep the page and the date for every address.
- Guessed addresses carry no implied consent, and collecting addresses with harvesting software runs into privacy law.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › What counts as a commercial electronic message
chunks.text:
CASL regulates commercial electronic messages, or CEMs. A CEM is an electronic message, such as an email or a text, that would reasonably be seen, from its content, its links or its contact details, as having the purpose, or one of the purposes, of encouraging participation in a commercial activity.
The Act names offers to sell a service, ads for one, and messages that promote someone as a provider. An email offering a café a new website, a booking page or a website audit is a CEM. A friendly introduction that links to your services can be one too, since links count.
Two details are easy to miss. An email asking for consent is itself a CEM (s. 1(3)), so it needs consent of its own. And the sending rules apply whenever a computer system in Canada is used to send or access the message (s. 12(1)), wherever the sender is based.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › Express and implied consent (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
Section 6 bans sending a CEM unless the person has consented, expressly or impliedly, and the message carries the required identification and unsubscribe mechanism.
Express consent
Express consent is a clear yes, given orally or in writing. The request must say why you’re asking, who is asking and how to reach you, and that consent can be withdrawn. It lasts until the person withdraws it.
Implied consent
The Act lists the only situations where consent is implied (s. 10(9)). Three matter most to agencies:
- An existing business relationship: the business bought from you in the last two years, or sent you an inquiry in the last six months

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › Express and implied consent (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
- An address given to you, such as on a business card, with no request to avoid unsolicited messages, when your message relates to the person’s business or role
- A conspicuously published address, covered in the next section
The regulations add a referral exemption: a first message after a referral needs no consent when the person who referred you has a business, non-business, family or personal relationship with both of you, and your message gives their full name and says it follows their referral.
Identification and unsubscribe rules still apply to that message. The business-to-business exemption needs the two organizations to already have a relationship, so it doesn’t cover a cold first email.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › Conspicuously published addresses
chunks.text:
Without a relationship, a business card or a referral, a cold email rests on section 10(9)(b). It implies consent only when all three conditions hold:
1. The address is conspicuously published: The person published it, or had it published, in plain view: a contact page or a site footer. A directory that copied it on its own doesn’t fit that wording, so go to the business’s own site.
2. Nothing refuses unsolicited messages: The publication can’t come with a statement that the person doesn’t want unsolicited commercial messages at that address. Check the page and the site’s legal notices for “no solicitation” wording.
3. Your message is relevant: It must relate to the person’s business, role, functions or duties in a business or official capacity. A website offer sent to a clinic’s reception address fits. A personal offer to whoever reads that inbox doesn’t.
Being visible online isn’t enough on its own. CRTC enforcement staff issued an advisory after seeing businesses email lists of addresses gathered from public websites. The Privacy Commissioner’s guidance adds that people post addresses for many purposes, so you can’t assume they want offers.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › What every message must include
chunks.text:
Consent isn’t the whole job. Every CEM must also identify the sender, give a way to reach them and include an unsubscribe mechanism (s. 6(2), s. 11 and the CRTC’s regulations).
Requirement | What it means:
- Who is sending: The name you do business under. Sending for a client? Name the client too, and say who is sending on whose behalf
- How to reach you: Your mailing address, plus a phone number that reaches a person or voicemail, an email address or a website. It must stay valid for at least 60 days after sending
- How to unsubscribe: At no cost to the person, by the same electronic means the message used, at an email address or web page you specify. Easy to do, and valid for at least 60 days
- How fast: Without delay, and no later than 10 business days after the request, with nothing more asked of the person
- Where it goes: Clearly and prominently in the message. Sender details that can’t practicably fit may sit on a web page behind a clear link

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › Keep records of consent
chunks.text:
Whoever claims consent has to prove it (s. 13). CRTC staff have seen senders unable to do so, and suggest keeping, among other records:
- Evidence of express and implied consent
- The methods you used to collect consent, documented
- Your policies and procedures for complying with CASL
- Every unsubscribe request, and what you did about it
For a published address, the evidence is the page: its web address, the date you saw it and what it said. The Privacy Commissioner also suggests revisiting records and their sources at intervals, to confirm that implied consent still holds.
The CRTC adds that good records can help establish a due diligence defence: a person isn’t liable for a violation if they show they exercised due diligence to prevent it (s. 33(1)).

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › CASL penalties
chunks.text:
The CRTC can impose administrative monetary penalties for violations of sections 6 to 9. The maximum is $1 million per violation for an individual and $10 million for any other person, such as a company (s. 20(4)).
The Act says penalties exist to promote compliance, not to punish. The amount depends on factors such as the nature and scope of the violation, past violations, any financial benefit and the ability to pay.
Liability spreads, too. Aiding or causing a violation is itself prohibited (s. 9), officers and directors who direct or authorize one can be liable (s. 31), and employers answer for employees acting within their employment (s. 32).

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › Harvested and guessed addresses
chunks.text:
CASL also amended PIPEDA, the federal private-sector privacy law. Its section 7.1 targets an individual’s address collected with a computer program designed or marketed primarily to generate or search for, and collect, electronic addresses.
For such an address, the exceptions that allow collection or use without consent don’t apply, the “publicly available” one included. The Privacy Commissioner’s guidance says that, with very limited exceptions, PIPEDA prohibits address harvesting, whether a tool scrapes websites or generates addresses from common names and email domains.
A bought list doesn’t get around it: the same guidance makes it your responsibility to check how a vendor collected its addresses. Québec, Alberta and British Columbia have their own private-sector privacy laws, which generally apply instead within those provinces, while PIPEDA covers information that crosses provincial or national borders.
Guessing fails under CASL as well. An address you built yourself, such as firstname.lastname@ plus the business’s domain, was never published by anyone, so the conspicuous-publication rule can’t cover it.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › A checklist before you write to a local business (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
1. Find the address at the source: Use the business’s own website: its contact page, footer or about page. Prefer a role address such as info@ or reception@ to a named person’s address.
2. Look for a refusal: A statement that the business doesn’t want unsolicited messages rules that address out.
3. Make it relevant: Pitch what relates to the business: its website, booking, listing or email setup.
4. Record where it came from: Note the page’s web address, the date and the address exactly as published. Keep a copy of the page if you can.
5. Identify yourself: Your business name, your mailing address, and a phone number, email address or website that will work for at least 60 days.

chunks.title: Guide: Cold email in Canada: what CASL requires of agencies › A checklist before you write to a local business (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
6. Offer an easy way out: An unsubscribe that costs nothing and takes one step. Honour it right away: 10 business days is the legal maximum, not a target.
7. Keep one opt-out list: Check it before every send, from every tool you send with.
8. Don’t guess, harvest or buy addresses: A guessed address has no implied consent, harvesting software runs into PIPEDA, and a bought list still leaves you answerable for how it was collected.
9. Recheck before the next campaign: Pages change. Revisit the source before you write again, and stop if the address is gone or a refusal has appeared.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
What SPF, DKIM and DMARC do, how to check any domain’s records, what Google and Yahoo require, and how to turn a weak result into a fair first email.
Published November 1, 2026. Topic: Audits.
Three DNS records tell mail servers whether email from a domain is genuine: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. For an agency they matter twice: a prospect’s weak setup is a real problem you can verify and help fix, and Google and Yahoo expect the same records on your own outreach.
In short:
- SPF lists who may send for a domain, DKIM signs each message, and DMARC checks that one of them matches the From address.
- All three are public DNS records: checking a domain sends it nothing.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
- Google and Yahoo require SPF or DKIM from every sender, and all three from bulk senders.
- Warning signs: no SPF, more than 10 DNS lookups, no DMARC, or p=none that never moves.
- Get your own domain right first, then point out one finding calmly, with the fix.
Search terms: spf, dkim, dmarc, email authentication, spf record, dkim selector, dmarc policy, p=none, dmarc alignment, too many dns lookups, permerror, dns txt record, google sender requirements, yahoo sender requirements, bulk sender, email deliverability, spam folder, check email setup, email health, cold email, casl, agency, freelancer

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › What SPF, DKIM and DMARC do (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
SPF: who may send
SPF (Sender Policy Framework, RFC 7208) is one TXT record on the domain that lists the servers allowed to send its email. Receivers look up the domain in the envelope sender, the return path most people never see, and check that the sending server is on its list.
v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all is the record Google documents for a domain that sends only through Google Workspace. Google’s servers may send; mail from any other server is probably not allowed.
At the end, -all fails every other server, ~all marks them as probably not allowed (Google recommends it), ?all stays neutral, and +all lets anyone send as the domain.
-all has a catch: RFC 9989 warns that it can get mail refused before DMARC sees its DKIM signature. Whatever the ending, keep to one record: only one TXT record on a domain may start with v=spf1.
DKIM: a signature on each message

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › What SPF, DKIM and DMARC do (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
With DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail, RFC 6376), the sending service signs each message. The receiver fetches the public key from DNS and checks the signature, which also shows the signed parts weren’t changed on the way.
The key lives at <selector>._domainkey.<yourdomain.ca>, and Google Workspace’s default selector is google. DNS can’t list selectors: to find one, view a message’s source and read s= in its DKIM-Signature header, alongside d=, the signing domain.
DMARC: the rule that ties them together
DMARC (RFC 9989, which replaced RFC 7489 in May 2026) is a TXT record at _dmarc.<yourdomain.ca>. It tells receivers what to do with mail that shows the domain in its From address but fails DMARC, and where to send reports.
v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:<reports address at yourdomain.ca> makes a good first record. Its policy, p=, takes one of three values:
- none: no preference, only reports. RFC 9989 calls this monitoring mode
- quarantine: treat failing mail as suspicious, which can mean the spam folder
- reject: refuse failing mail

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › How they work together: alignment
chunks.text:
SPF and DKIM each vouch for a domain, but not always the one people see. A scammer can pass SPF for a domain they own while showing yours in the From line. DMARC closes that gap with alignment.
A message passes DMARC when SPF or DKIM passes and the domain it passed for matches the From domain. With relaxed alignment, the default, a subdomain counts: news.<yourdomain.ca> aligns with <yourdomain.ca>. Strict alignment (adkim=s or aspf=s) needs the exact domain.
One aligned pass is enough, and RFC 9989 asks for two where possible. Lean on DKIM: forwarded mail will most likely fail SPF unless the forwarder rewrites the return path, while DKIM signatures generally survive.
[Note] When a sending service fails DMARC: If a newsletter or booking tool uses its own domain for the return path and for its DKIM signature, both checks can pass but neither matches your From domain, so DMARC fails. Set the tool to sign with your domain.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › How to check any domain (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
It’s all public, so checking a domain sends nothing to its owner. The quickest way is our email check (/email-check/): type a domain and it reads MX, SPF, DKIM and DMARC from your browser in a few seconds, with what to fix.
By hand
1. Look up the SPF record: In a terminal, run nslookup -type=TXT <domain.ca> on Windows or dig +short TXT <domain.ca> on a Mac, and find the record that starts with v=spf1.
2. Look up the DMARC record: Do the same for _dmarc.<domain.ca>. No record starting with v=DMARC1 means no DMARC.
3. Look up a DKIM key: With the selector from a message’s s= value, look up <selector>._domainkey.<domain.ca>. No answer under a guessed name proves nothing.
With Email health in RadiusPilot
In RadiusPilot, open Tools › Email health, enter a domain, an email address or a website, or pick a business you scanned, and choose Check email. It reads public DNS in a few seconds, in the Windows app or the web app (/web/).
Record | What Email health reads and flags:

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › How to check any domain (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
- MX: Receives email: the mail servers and who runs them. Flags a domain with none, since mail to it bounces.
- SPF: Allowed senders: the record, the services it allows and its own lookups. Flags no record or several, +all, a neutral or missing ending, and over 10 lookups.
- DKIM: Signed email: keys under 22 common selectors, with a rough size. Flags a key switched off (empty p=); none found reads Unknown, not Missing.
- DMARC: Protection from fakes: the policy and the report address. Flags no record or several, no valid policy, p=none, test mode (t=y) and the retired pct below 100.
You get a verdict (Healthy, Needs work or At risk), a What to fix list, starter records when SPF or DMARC is missing, and a pitch line built only from the check.
If the domain is a business’s website in your workspace, the result is saved on that business and feeds its website audit (/help/website-checks/#diagnosis) and opportunity score (/help/opportunity-score/). The audit runs Email health too, even across a whole scan with Audit several.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › What a weak result looks like (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
Act on these, on any domain, yours included.
What you see | What it means, and the fix:
- No SPF record: Receivers can’t tell who may send for the domain. Fix: publish one record listing every sender.
- Two SPF records: Only one is allowed, so SPF returns an error. Fix: merge them into one.
- +all at the end: Any server in the world may send as the domain. Fix: end with ~all or -all.
- Over 10 DNS lookups: SPF returns an error and can’t pass. Fix: remove what the domain no longer uses.
- No DMARC record: Nothing asks receivers to act on fakes. Fix: add p=none with reports, then move up.
- p=none for months: Receivers are asked to do nothing about fakes. Fix: act on the reports, then move to quarantine.
- No DKIM key found: Unsigned mail, or a custom selector. Fix: turn on signing in the email service.
Too many DNS lookups
Each include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect in an SPF record costs a DNS lookup, and so does each one inside the records it includes. RFC 7208 caps the total at 10. ip4, ip6 and all don’t count.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › What a weak result looks like (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
To get back under, drop services the domain no longer uses, and any ptr, which RFC 7208 says not to publish. Email health counts the record’s own lookups; includes add theirs, so check them when the count nears 10.
A DMARC policy stuck at none
Starting at p=none is right: it’s the time to read reports and fix the domain’s own mail. Left there, it asks receivers to do nothing about mail that fakes the domain.
RFC 9989 warns that p=reject can break mail sent through mailing lists and forwarders, and requires DKIM signing from domains that use it. Before p=reject, it suggests a month or more at p=none, then as long at p=quarantine, comparing reports.
To try a stricter policy, RFC 9989 replaces the old pct= tag with test mode, t=y: receivers then apply one level less, so reject acts as quarantine and quarantine as none. Email health shows both as warnings. Remove pct=, and remove t=y once the reports are clean.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › What Google and Yahoo require (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
Since February 2024, Google and Yahoo have set requirements for mail to their users, with a longer list for bulk senders.
- Authentication: Every sender SPF or DKIM; Bulk senders SPF and DKIM
- DMARC: Every sender Recommended by both; Bulk senders Required; p=none is accepted
- Alignment: Every sender Not required; Bulk senders From aligned with SPF or DKIM
- Unsubscribe: Every sender Not required; Bulk senders One-click, plus a visible link
- Spam rate: Every sender Below 0.3%; Bulk senders Below 0.3%
- Sending servers: Every sender Forward and reverse DNS; Bulk senders The same
- Encryption: Every sender TLS, for Gmail; Bulk senders TLS, for Gmail

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › What Google and Yahoo require (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
Google counts as bulk anyone who sends more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts; Yahoo’s requirements page gives no number. The unsubscribe rules cover marketing and subscribed messages, and Yahoo wants them honoured within 2 days.
Google requires DKIM keys of 1024 bits or longer for personal Gmail accounts and recommends 2048 bits, and Yahoo recommends at least 1024. Email health shows each key’s rough size.
RadiusPilot’s daily limit starts at 50 people and never passes 200, far below Google’s bulk threshold. Google still recommends all three records for every domain: unauthenticated mail might be marked as spam or rejected.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › Get your own domain right first
chunks.text:
Check yours before you point out anyone else’s.
1. List every service that sends as you: Your mailbox, plus any newsletter, invoicing, booking or form tool using your domain.
2. Publish one SPF record: Include each service, end with ~all, and stay within 10 lookups.
3. Turn on DKIM everywhere: Have each service sign with your own domain, so DKIM aligns.
4. Add DMARC in monitoring mode: v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:<reports address at yourdomain.ca> goes in a TXT record named _dmarc. Reports are built for software, so a report-reading service helps.
5. Move up when the reports are clean: Once every service passes, switch to p=quarantine, then run Email health again.

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › Turn a weak result into a first email (part 1 of 2)
chunks.text:
A weak record is a fact anyone can verify: a fair reason to write, if you stay useful rather than alarming.
- Lead with one finding, in plain words, and how you found it: public DNS records, nothing sent to their servers.
- Say what it allows, no more. “Nothing tells mail servers to refuse email that fakes your address” is accurate; “you’ve been hacked” isn’t.
- Name the fix: a DNS change, by whoever manages the domain or the email.
- Leave out what you couldn’t confirm, like a DKIM key under a guessed selector.
- Check again the day you send. Records change.
[Note] A first email, in four lines: Hi <name>, I looked up the public email records for <domain.ca>. There’s no DMARC record, so nothing tells mail servers to refuse email that fakes a <domain.ca> address. It’s a small DNS change, and I can set it up or walk your web person through it. Would that help? <signature>
The rules in Canada

chunks.title: Guide: SPF, DKIM and DMARC explained for agency owners › Turn a weak result into a first email (part 2 of 2)
chunks.text:
CASL, Canada’s anti-spam law, covers commercial email sent from or opened on a computer in Canada, wherever you’re based. Implied consent can come from an address a business publishes conspicuously, with no statement refusing unsolicited messages, when your email relates to its business.
Each message must identify you, give contact details valid for at least 60 days, and offer an unsubscribe you honour within 10 business days. RadiusPilot adds your business name, postal address and unsubscribe line to every email, blocks your opt-out list and stops at your daily limit.
Published contacts (/help/published-contacts/) keeps the page where a business published its address, as your record. The email rules guide (/help/email-rules/) covers the rest.
[Warning] Not legal advice: This is general information about Canada’s anti-spam law. Ask a lawyer about your own outreach.
Email health is one of the eight tools (/tools/#email) in RadiusPilot. Try it in the web app (/web/), on your own domain first.

In the Windows app you can use your own account instead: Codex on your PC, your ChatGPT plan or an OpenAI API key. What it writes is labelled “AI-generated”, and you decide what gets sent. Where is my data kept?

Is there a Mac version?
